title: Ride the panic wave
text: Panic usually passes, often within 5 to 20 minutes. Remind yourself: this is a wave, not danger. Stay where you are if you can, slow your breathing a little, and focus on one thing nearby until it eases.

source.name: NHS: Panic disorder - NHS

title: Name the worry
text: Try saying it plainly: "I'm feeling anxious about ___." Naming a feeling can take some of its power away. Then ask: is this something I can act on today, or something I can only set down for now?

source.name: UCLA Newsroom (Lieberman et al. neuroimaging study): Putting Feelings Into Words Produces Therapeutic Effects in the Brain; UCLA Neuroimaging Study Supports Ancient Buddhist Teachings

title: 5-4-3-2-1 grounding
text: Look around and name 5 things you can see, 4 you can touch, 3 you can hear, 2 you can smell, and 1 you can taste. It pulls your attention out of your head and back into the room.

source.name: University of Rochester Medical Center, Behavioral Health Partners: 5-4-3-2-1 Coping Technique for Anxiety

title: Feel your feet
text: Press your feet firmly into the floor and notice the pressure. Hold something cool, like a glass of water or a cold cloth, and focus on how it feels. Small physical sensations can steady a racing mind.

source.name: San Diego State University Counseling & Psychological Services: Grounding Techniques

title: Longer breath out
text: Breathe in gently through your nose for about 4 counts, then out slowly for about 6. Slow, steady breathing can help your body settle. Try 5 or 6 rounds, and pause if you feel dizzy.

source.name: NHS: Breathing exercises for stress - NHS

title: Box breathing
text: Picture a square. Breathe in for 4, hold for 4, breathe out for 4, hold for 4. Trace the square in your mind as you go. It gives your attention something steady to follow.

source.name: Cleveland Clinic: How Box Breathing Can Help You Destress

title: Study in small chunks
text: Big exams feel huge because they are one big blob. Break it into small chunks, like one topic for 25 minutes, then a 5 minute break. Finishing one small piece builds momentum and makes the rest feel doable.

source.name: Kansas State University Academic Achievement Center: Pomodoro Study Method

title: Look at the realistic picture
text: When your mind says "I'll fail everything," try writing the worst case, the best case, and the most likely case. The likely one is often less scary than it feels. Then pick one thing you can do today.

source.name: University of Alabama at Birmingham: Five common thinking traps and what to think instead

title: One small reach-out
text: Loneliness is a signal that you want connection, not a flaw in you. Try one tiny step: send a short message to someone, wave to a neighbor, or join a low-pressure activity. Small contact adds up.

source.name: NHS Every Mind Matters: Loneliness - Every Mind Matters - NHS (page heading: Dealing with loneliness)

title: Be a good companion to yourself
text: On lonely evenings, plan something small that feels kind: a favorite meal, music, a walk outside, or a show you love. Treat the time as company you give yourself, and let it be gentle.

source.name: TODO: verify against source

title: A gentle wind-down
text: About an hour before bed, dim the lights and put your phone away. Do something slow, like stretching, a warm shower, or reading something light. Regular, quiet routines tell your body that night is for resting.

source.name: Sleep Foundation: How to Build a Better Bedtime Routine for Adults | Sleep Foundation

title: Brain dump before bed
text: If your mind races at night, keep a notebook by the bed. Write down what's circling, plus one small step for tomorrow. Putting thoughts on paper gives your mind permission to let go for the night.

source.name: NHS Every Mind Matters: How to fall asleep faster and sleep better

title: Make room for grief
text: Grief has no schedule and no right way. Waves of sadness, numbness, or even anger are all normal. Let yourself feel what comes, talk about the person if you want to, and be patient with how slowly it moves.

source.name: NHS: Grief after bereavement or loss - NHS

title: Protect small pockets of rest
text: When you're running on empty, rest has to be planned, not earned. Protect a few small pockets each day, like a short walk, a real lunch break, or ten quiet minutes. Rest is part of doing well, not a reward.

source.name: NHS Every Mind Matters: Work-related stress

title: Drop or shrink one thing
text: Look at your list and ask: what could I drop, delay, or do at 70% this week? You don't have to do everything at full effort. Easing one commitment can free up more energy than you'd expect.

source.name: NHS Every Mind Matters: Work-related stress

title: Pause before reacting
text: Anger carries energy that needs somewhere to go. Before you respond, pause: step away, take a few slow breaths, or move your body with a brisk walk. Come back to the conversation once the heat has dropped a little.

source.name: NHS: Get help with anger - NHS

title: What's under the anger?
text: Anger often sits on top of something softer, like hurt, fear, or feeling disrespected. Ask yourself: what am I really upset about, and what do I need? Naming it can help you say it calmly.

source.name: TODO: verify against source

title: Start with two minutes
text: Starting is the hardest part. Tell yourself you'll work on it for just two minutes, then you're allowed to stop. Most of the time, starting breaks the resistance and you'll keep going a bit longer.

source.name: University of Iowa University Counseling Service: Procrastination Self-help Workshop | University Counseling Service - Division of Student Life | The University of Iowa

title: Make the first step tiny
text: Big tasks feel scary because they're vague. Shrink the first step until it's almost silly, like opening the document and typing a title. Do that one thing, then choose the next small step.

source.name: University of Iowa University Counseling Service: Procrastination Self-help Workshop | University Counseling Service - Division of Student Life | The University of Iowa

title: Cool down, then talk
text: Family arguments feel intense because the relationships matter. If things are heated, take a break first. Later, try "I feel ___ when ___, and I'd like ___." If you ever feel unsafe, step away and reach out for support.

source.name: Utah State University Extension: During the Fight: Perspectives and Skills for De-escalating Conflicts

title: Talk to yourself like a friend
text: Imagine a close friend made the same mistake. What would you say to them? Try saying that to yourself. You can hold high standards and still be kind about being human.

source.name: Greater Good Science Center, UC Berkeley: How Would You Treat a Friend?

title: Thought, not fact
text: A harsh thought like "I'm a failure" feels true but is still just a thought. Try rewording it: "I'm having the thought that I'm a failure." Then look for one piece of evidence that doesn't fit.

source.name: Northwestern University (CSAW): Defusion Techniques

title: Get it out of your head
text: When everything feels like too much, write every task and worry on paper without sorting. Then circle just one thing for today. Seeing it all on paper can make it feel more manageable than it did in your head.

source.name: NHS: Get help with stress - NHS

title: Just the next small thing
text: You don't have to solve it all right now. Ask: what is the next small thing I can do in the next ten minutes? Do just that, then ask again. Steady small steps can get you through a heavy day.

source.name: University of Colorado Boulder, Division of Student Life: 5 ways to manage stress during midterms | Division of Student Life | University of Colorado Boulder

title: Set a worry window
text: If worries keep looping, set aside a 10 minute worry window each day. When a worry pops up outside it, jot it down and tell yourself you'll think about it later. This helps your mind trust it won't be forgotten.

source.name: NHS Every Mind Matters: Tackling your worries - Every Mind Matters - NHS

title: Let heartbreak be real
text: Heartbreak is a real loss, and it can ache like grief. You don't have to rush to feel better. Let the sadness come in waves, cry if you need to, and be gentle with yourself while it settles.

source.name: Loyola University Maryland Counseling Center: Break-Ups | Counseling Center | Loyola University Maryland

title: Give your heart some space
text: The urge to check an ex's messages or profiles is normal, and checking can make it harder to heal. Consider muting or pausing contact for a while. It isn't punishment, it just gives your heart room to heal.

source.name: UT Dallas Student Counseling Center: Coping with a Breakup – Student Counseling Center | UT Dallas

title: Small daily anchors
text: When a relationship ends, days can feel shapeless. Anchor them with small basics: eat something, step outside, move a little, sleep at regular times. These aren't fixes, just steady ground while you grieve.

source.name: NHS: Get help with grief after bereavement or loss - NHS

title: When love isn't returned
text: Not being chosen hurts, but it says something about fit, not your worth. Let yourself feel the disappointment, then turn some of that care back toward yourself and the people who already value you.

source.name: TODO: verify against source

title: Ghosted and wondering why
text: Being ghosted leaves you without answers, and your mind fills the gap with blame. Their silence reflects their choices, not your value. You can decide you've waited enough and move on without closure.

source.name: University of Colorado Boulder, Health Center: Been ghosted? Check out these tips

title: When your parents split up
text: A parent split can shake your sense of home, even if you saw it coming. It's okay to feel sad, angry, or relieved, sometimes all at once. You didn't cause it, and you're allowed to ask for support.

source.name: Boston Children's Hospital, Center for Young Women's Health: Dealing with Divorce and Separation

title: One day at a time
text: When life is heavy, planning far ahead can feel impossible. Shrink your focus to today: what is one thing that would make it a little bit easier? Getting through this day is enough.

source.name: NHS: Help for suicidal thoughts

title: Hold on to one steady thing
text: In a stormy stretch, hold on to one steady thing, like a daily walk, a favorite song, or a call with someone who knows you. A small constant gives you something solid when everything else shifts.

source.name: TODO: verify against source

title: Feelings shift over time
text: Hopelessness can make this moment feel permanent, but feelings can change over time, even when it doesn't seem possible. Focus on getting through today, and consider telling someone you trust how heavy things feel.

source.name: NHS: Help for suicidal thoughts

title: Bankruptcy isn't a verdict on you
text: Money trouble is stressful and can bring heavy shame, but financial setbacks happen to many people and say nothing about your worth. Take it one practical step at a time, and free advice is available.

source.name: NHS Every Mind Matters: Money worries and mental health

title: Face the numbers gently
text: Avoiding money worries can let them grow. Set aside a calm time to write down what you owe and what's coming in. Seeing the real numbers can be a first step to a plan, and free advice can help.

source.name: NHS Every Mind Matters: Money worries and mental health

title: Ask the right kind of help
text: Money and legal questions are worth taking to people who know them well. Look for free or low-cost financial counseling or legal aid in your area, and ask someone you trust to sit with you through the paperwork.

source.name: NHS: Coping with financial worries

title: After losing a job
text: Losing a job can shake your confidence, routine, and income all at once. It's okay to grieve it. Keep a simple daily structure, tell a few people you trust, and take job-hunting steps in small pieces.

source.name: TODO: verify against source

title: When you get turned down
text: A rejection stings, and it's fine to feel disappointed for a bit. One no is about one decision at one moment, not your whole future. Give yourself time, then choose one small next step.

source.name: TODO: verify against source

title: Failure is information
text: A failure feels final in the moment, but it also tells you something about what to change. Ask gently: what's one thing I learned, and what's one thing I'd try differently? Then give yourself credit for trying.

source.name: TODO: verify against source

title: Losing a friend hurts
text: Friendship breakups are real losses, yet they often get less comfort than romantic ones. It's okay to grieve what you shared. People can also drift apart without anyone being the villain.

source.name: TODO: verify against source

title: Betrayed by a friend
text: Being betrayed by a friend hurts deeply because you trusted them. Your anger and sadness make sense. You get to decide how much trust to give next, and it's okay to protect yourself for now.

source.name: TODO: verify against source

title: Thinking about repairing it
text: If you miss the friendship, a short, honest message can open a door: say what you value, own your part, and don't demand anything back right away. They may not reply, and that's okay. You reached out with care.

source.name: TODO: verify against source

title: Left out of the group
text: Being left out stings, and it can make you question yourself. It doesn't have to mean something is wrong with you. Look for one person or space where you feel relaxed, and slowly build from there.

source.name: Cornell Chronicle (Cornell University): Talking with a friend can ease the sting of being left out

title: Regret shows what you value
text: Regret can hurt because you care. Try separating "I did something I regret" from "I'm a terrible person." Guilt about an action can point toward repair, while harsh self-judgment tends to feel heavier and less useful.

source.name: PubMed Central (Behavioral Sciences, Dempsey review): A Comparison of the Social-Adaptive Perspective and Functionalist Perspective on Guilt and Shame

title: Facing emotional cheating
text: Crossing a line in a relationship, even emotionally, can bring heavy guilt. Be honest with yourself about what happened and what you were looking for. Own it without self-punishment, and consider a counselor to help with next steps.

source.name: TODO: verify against source

title: When a partner cheated
text: Finding out about cheating can feel like the ground vanished. Shock, rage, and grief are all normal. You don't have to decide anything right away. Lean on someone you trust, and give yourself time before big choices.

source.name: TODO: verify against source

title: Taking responsibility
text: A real apology names what you did, acknowledges how it affected them, and asks what repair could look like, without excuses or demands for forgiveness. Do your part, and accept that healing runs on their timeline.

source.name: Greater Good Science Center, UC Berkeley: Making an Effective Apology

title: Forgiving yourself
text: Forgiving yourself doesn't mean what happened was okay. It means you stop punishing yourself and use what you learned. Ask: what would I need to do, or change, to carry this more lightly?

source.name: Greater Good Science Center, UC Berkeley: Why Forgiving Ourselves Feels So Hard—and What Helps

title: Choices you can't undo
text: It's painful to look back and see the road you didn't take. You made your choices with what you knew then. Try asking what the regret is asking of you now, and whether there's a small step you can still take.

source.name: Cleveland Clinic: How To Deal With Regrets

title: If you're being bullied
text: Being bullied is not your fault, and you don't have to handle it alone. Tell someone you trust, like a teacher, counselor, or family member, and keep a record of what happened. You deserve to feel safe.

source.name: Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust (CAMHS): Bullying - CAMHS

title: If a relationship feels unsafe
text: If someone makes you afraid, controls who you see, or hurts you, it is not your fault, and you deserve safety. Please reach out to someone you trust or a local support service. If you're in danger now, contact emergency services.

source.name: NHS: Getting help for domestic violence and abuse - NHS

title: Missing home
text: Missing home is a sign of how much those people and places matter. Keep small links alive, like a regular call or a familiar meal, while also giving the new place small chances, like one class or one coffee, to become yours.

source.name: Lafayette College Counseling Center: Homesickness

title: Comparison and envy
text: Comparing yourself to others usually pits your behind-the-scenes against their highlight reel. Notice what the envy points to that you want, then take one small step toward it. Consider muting accounts that leave you feeling worse.

source.name: Penn State (student psychology blog) plus Manchester NHS CAMHS: The Psychology Behind Social Media Envy

title: Dreading social situations
text: Worry about being judged is common. Start small: one short chat, one comment in class. Notice how it actually went, and be kind to yourself afterward.

source.name: NHS: Social anxiety (social phobia) - NHS

title: Body image struggles
text: Your worth isn't tied to how you look, even when your mind insists it is. Notice what your body does for you, wear what feels comfortable, and be careful with feeds that leave you feeling worse about yourself.

source.name: Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust (CAMHS): Body Image - CAMHS

title: Waiting on health news
text: Waiting on health news is frightening. Focus on what you can control, like writing down questions for your doctor and having someone with you. Try not to spend hours searching online; your care team can give reliable answers.

source.name: NHS: Health anxiety

title: Caring for someone else
text: Caring for someone you love is demanding, and feeling tired or resentful doesn't make you a bad person. Ask for help with one concrete task, protect a little time for yourself, and share how heavy it is with someone.

source.name: Oxford Health NHS Foundation Trust: Getting the support you need

title: Feeling lost about who you are
tags: what to do with my life
text: Not knowing who you are or where you're headed can be unsettling, but it's also a normal stretch of growing up. You don't need the whole map. Try small experiments and notice what gives you energy.

source.name: Loyola University Maryland Counseling Center: Who am I? How do Others View Me?

title: Feeling like you let people down
text: The fear of letting people down can feel crushing. Remember that you're a person, not a performance. Consider telling someone you trust what pressure you feel, and decide which expectations you actually want to carry.

source.name: TODO: verify against source

title: Feeling numb
text: Numbness can be your mind's way of coping with too much. It isn't a failing. Try small sensory comforts like warmth, music, or a walk, and stay in touch with someone you trust. If it lasts, a counselor can help.

source.name: Cleveland Clinic: Emotional Numbness: What Causes It and What To Do About It

title: It's okay to cry
text: Crying is a natural response to stress and sadness, and it often brings some relief. You don't have to hold it in or explain it. Let it come, then maybe drink some water and do one small, gentle thing for yourself.

source.name: Cleveland Clinic: Why You May Feel Better After Crying

title: Preparing for a hard conversation
text: Before a hard conversation, jot down the one thing you most want them to understand and how you'd like to say it. Pick a calm time and place, use "I" statements, and let there be pauses.

source.name: TODO: verify against source

title: Reaching out is okay
text: Many people worry about being a burden, but most are glad to be trusted. Start small: "I've been having a hard time. Can I talk?" The right person will want to listen, and you deserve that.

source.name: Samaritans: TALK tips: how to open up and talk about how you are feeling | Samaritans

title: Feeling like a fraud
text: Feeling like a fraud is common, especially in new or competitive places, and many people around you quietly feel it too. Keep a short list of things you've handled well, and read it when the doubt gets loud.

source.name: University of Colorado Denver: Imposter Syndrome: When You Feel Like a Fraud

title: Failing a class
text: A bad grade can feel like a disaster, but it's usually more fixable than it seems. Talk to the instructor or an academic advisor soon, since they often know options you don't. One class or semester doesn't define your path.

source.name: TODO: verify against source

title: Thinking about changing course
text: Questioning your path is normal and doesn't mean you've failed. Before deciding, talk it through with an advisor and someone who knows you well. Ask what you'd be moving toward, not just what you'd be escaping.

source.name: University of Northern Iowa Academic Advising: Thinking about Changing Your Major?

title: Living with waiting
text: Waiting is hard because your mind keeps trying to solve something it can't solve yet. Give the worry a short daily check-in time, then turn to something absorbing. You'll handle the answer when it comes.

source.name: NHS Every Mind Matters: Tackling your worries - Every Mind Matters - NHS

title: Tension with a roommate
text: Living closely with someone lets small irritations pile up. Pick a calm moment, raise one specific issue, and suggest a simple fix you could both try. Agreeing on a few house rules can prevent bigger fights later.

source.name: University of North Florida Housing: Conflict Resolution Tips

title: A hard job or boss
text: A difficult job can follow you home. Keep notes on problems, set limits where you can, like not answering messages late at night, and lean on people outside work. You're allowed to look for something better while you stay.

source.name: NHS: Get help with stress - NHS

title: Nerves before an interview
text: Nerves before an interview mean you care. Prepare a few short stories about times you handled something well, practice them out loud, and plan your route. Remember it's also your chance to decide if they're right for you.

source.name: TODO: verify against source

title: Long-distance strain
text: Distance makes small gaps feel bigger. Plan regular calls you can both count on, share little everyday moments, and keep a visit on the calendar to look forward to. It's okay to talk honestly about how hard it feels.

source.name: TODO: verify against source

title: Mixed signals
text: Not knowing where you stand can be exhausting. You're allowed to ask for clarity, kindly and directly. Their answer, or their silence, gives you information, and you can decide what you need from there.

source.name: TODO: verify against source

title: Insecurity in a relationship
text: Relationship worries can spiral into checking and needing reassurance. Notice the fear, breathe, and ask what has actually happened versus what you're imagining. Then share what you need calmly, rather than testing your partner.

source.name: TODO: verify against source

title: When you were the one who ended it
text: Ending a relationship can bring guilt and grief, even when it was the right call. You can care about someone and still know it wasn't working. Let yourself miss them while trusting the reasons you had.

source.name: NHS: Get help with grief after bereavement or loss - NHS

title: Losing a pet
text: Losing a pet can feel like losing a family member, and the grief can be intense. It's okay to cry, keep their things for a while, or make a small memorial. Your grief is real, even if others don't understand.

source.name: Cleveland Clinic: How to Grieve the Death of a Pet

title: Anniversaries and reminders
text: Anniversaries, holidays, and small reminders can bring grief rushing back. That doesn't mean you're going backwards. Plan something gentle for those days, like visiting a place or spending time with people who remember too.

source.name: NHS: Get help with grief after bereavement or loss - NHS

title: Facing discrimination
text: Being treated unfairly for who you are is painful, and it is not your fault. Your anger and hurt make sense. Write down what happened, find people who understand, and know you can report it to someone with the power to act.

source.name: TODO: verify against source

title: Exploring who you are
text: Exploring your sexuality or gender is a personal journey with no deadline. You get to decide who to tell and when, and your safety comes first. Look for affirming people or communities where you can be fully yourself.

source.name: TODO: verify against source

title: After something frightening
text: After something frightening, it's normal to feel shaky, jumpy, or keep replaying it. Be gentle with yourself, stay near people you trust, and keep basic routines. If memories keep disrupting your life, talking to a professional can really help.

source.name: NIMH: Coping With Traumatic Events

title: If someone hurt you sexually
text: If someone did something sexual without your consent, it is not your fault, and you deserve care. Consider telling someone you trust or contacting a local sexual assault support service. If you're hurt or in danger, please seek emergency or medical help.

source.name: TODO: verify against source

title: Leaning on drinking or substances
text: Using alcohol or other substances to cope is common, and it often makes hard feelings heavier later. Without judging yourself, notice when and why you reach for it. A doctor or support service can help if cutting back feels hard.

source.name: NHS: Alcohol support - NHS

title: Gambling losses
text: Losing money on gambling or risky bets can bring panic and shame. Pause before trying to win it back, since chasing losses usually deepens them. Tell someone you trust, and look for a gambling support service if it's hard to stop.

source.name: NHS: Help for problems with gambling - NHS

title: When food feels like a battle
text: If food, eating, or weight feel like a constant battle, you're not alone, and you deserve support, not judgment. A doctor or counselor can help, and it's worth reaching out soon, even if you're unsure it's serious.

source.name: NHS: Overview - Eating disorders - NHS

title: When nothing feels enjoyable
text: When nothing feels enjoyable, it can help to try one tiny pleasant thing anyway, like music, sunlight, or texting a friend, and notice any small shift. If this low mood lasts weeks, a doctor or counselor can help.

source.name: NHS: Overview - Depression in adults - NHS

title: Feeling unwanted
text: Feeling unwanted is deeply painful, and it makes the mind notice only evidence that fits. Try to recall one person who has shown you care, even in a small way. Reaching out to them, or to a counselor, can ease the isolation.

source.name: TODO: verify against source

title: Heavy news and world events
text: Hard news can make the world feel overwhelming. It's okay to set limits, like checking once a day and avoiding it close to bedtime. Turn some worry into a small action if it helps, and spend time on things that ground you.

source.name: CDC: Managing Stress | Mental Health | CDC

title: Replaying an embarrassing moment
text: Replaying an awkward moment makes it feel huge, but other people usually forget it far faster than you do. Ask how you'd see it if a friend did the same thing. Then let it become a story you might laugh at later.

source.name: TODO: verify against source

title: Money stress at home
text: Seeing your family struggle with money can make you feel guilty or responsible. It isn't yours to fix alone. Ask your school's financial aid office about options, and talk honestly with family about what you can and can't carry.

source.name: TODO: verify against source

title: When an injury takes you out
text: Being sidelined by injury can take away your routine, identity, and the people you train with. It's normal to grieve that. Stay connected with your team, set small recovery goals, and find other ways to feel like yourself meanwhile.

source.name: TODO: verify against source

title: Distance from family
text: Distance from family, chosen or not, can bring grief and loneliness, especially around holidays. Relief and sadness can both be true. Build a circle of people who feel like family, and reach out to local services if you need housing or safety help.

source.name: TODO: verify against source

title: Lonely holidays
text: Holidays can highlight what's missing. Plan something small that feels kind, connect with even one person, and remember many people feel this way quietly. It's one day, and you can get through it in your own way.

source.name: TODO: verify against source
